cards.back: Functional says what a user can do (shorten a URL). Non-functional says under what load, how fast, how reliably and at what cost, and that is what decides caches, queues, sharding and regions.
An SLI is what you measure (share of requests under 300 ms), an SLO is the target for it (99.9% over 30 days), and an SLA is a contract with consequences, usually looser than the SLO.
The gap between 100% and the SLO. At 99.9% that is about 43 minutes of failure a month you can spend on deploys, experiments and bad luck.
An 80 ms average can hide a 2 s p99. A page making 50 backend calls hits at least one call's p99 on about 40% of loads, so tail latency is what users feel.
How much recent data you may lose. An RPO of zero needs synchronous replication before acknowledging a write; 5 minutes can be met with async replication or log shipping.
How long until service is back. Minutes needs a warm standby that can take traffic; hours can be met by restoring from backups.
About 22 minutes of downtime a month.
Roughly ten times as much effort. Ask what downtime actually costs the business before defaulting to five nines.
The evening peak or the sale day, typically 3 to 10× the average, not the daily mean.
Write latency, because each write must wait for copies in another zone or region.

cards.front: How many checklist rows to use
cards.back: Pick the three or four that will shape the design, not every row for every problem.

quiz.q: A team says the system must be 'highly available and scalable'. What is the most useful next step?
choices: Turn it into numbers such as 99.95% and 50k reads/s at peak
Add a second region straight away
Accept it as the requirement and start drawing
quiz.why: Adjectives decide nothing; numbers like a nines target and peak throughput do.

quiz.q: Your SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. Roughly how much failure can you spend each month?
quiz.why: The error budget at 99.9% is about 43 minutes a month.

quiz.q: Average latency is 80 ms but users complain the page is slow. The page makes 50 backend calls. What should you look at?
choices: Average CPU on the web tier
The p99 of the backend calls
quiz.why: With 50 calls, about 40% of page loads hit at least one call's p99, so tail latency is what users feel.

quiz.q: The business says no acknowledged write may ever be lost, even if a zone fails. What does that require?
choices: Synchronous replication to another zone before acknowledging
quiz.why: An RPO of zero needs the write copied synchronously before it is acknowledged, at the cost of slower writes.

quiz.q: An interviewer wants checkout and the product page designed. Which consistency choice fits best?
quiz.why: Most systems need strong consistency in one or two places, such as checkout to avoid overselling, and eventual elsewhere.

quiz.q: Daily mean traffic is 10k requests/s. What should capacity plans be based on?
choices: The evening or sale-day peak, often 3 to 10× the mean
quiz.why: Size for the peak, not the mean.

quiz.q: A recovery plan needs service back within minutes after a region loss. Which setup meets that RTO?
choices: A warm standby that can take traffic
Asynchronous replication with no standby compute
quiz.why: An RTO of minutes needs a warm standby; restoring from backups takes hours.
